sentences.text: Rosa went to the top shelf behind the counter.
She took down a very large old leather-bound ledger.
It was Angus's — the shop had had many owners, but the ledger had been passed down through all of them.
Rosa carried it to the counter.
Iona followed.
Rosa opened it to a page near the back.
She showed Iona a small handwritten note in old careful cursive.
It read: 12 May 1968.
Bought lot of eleven books from estate of Sir Walter Balfour of Balfour Farm.
Small collection.
Four of the eleven have last chapter torn out — same rough tearing pattern in all four.
Titles: Cecil Wray (1889), The Silence of Ellen Grey (1901), Meadowbank (1912), Northshore (1928).
Cannot say when tearing was done.
Books catalogued under 'incomplete' — will not sell without warning purchaser.
Waited two months to see if buyer would come for them.
Nobody did.
Storing them in the back cupboard for now.
If more arrive from the same farm someday, will note here.
Iona was quiet.
She said, "And they never sold?" Rosa nodded.
"They are still here.
I found them in the back cupboard my first month at the shop.
All four of them.
Exactly where he had put them fifty-nine years ago." She got up.
She went to a small cupboard at the back of the counter area.
She unlocked it with a small key.
She reached in.
She took out four old books, wrapped together in soft cloth.
She brought them to Iona.
Iona unwrapped them.
There they were — Cecil Wray, Silence of Ellen Grey, Meadowbank, Northshore.
Same tearing pattern.
Same clean removal of the last chapter.
Iona held one in her hand.
She said, quietly, "So somebody at that farm was tearing the last chapter out of novels.
For — for how long?" Rosa said, "Well.
The four Angus bought were from a 1960s estate.
So those books were being torn — sometime before 1968.
The seven we just got are from Mrs.
Balfour's estate.
She died last month.
She was ninety-three.
So — since her father's time, at the earliest.
Ninety years ago?
Maybe.
And still happening as of not long ago.
That is — that is a lot of years of one person tearing endings out of novels."
"But why," Iona said.
"Why would anyone do that." Rosa said, "I have thought about this a lot.
I have three ideas.
First — it could be someone who did not like endings.
Some people don't.
Some people like to imagine what happens.
Some people find endings disappointing.
So they tore them out.
That is a possibility." "Second?" said Iona.
Rosa said, "Second — it could be someone who thought the endings were wrong.
Not just disappointing — actually wrong.
As if the book had let itself down.
That is a specific kind of reader.
A person who takes the story so seriously that a bad ending feels like a betrayal."
"Third?" "Third," said Rosa, "and this is the one I actually think — it could be someone who thought that endings were — private.
That every reader should be allowed to make their own ending.
That the printed ending was — an intrusion.
An answer to a question that should not have been answered by the author.
Only by the reader.
That is a strange idea.
But some people have it." She paused.
"If it was the third one — if it was someone who thought that — they were making a small quiet argument, book by book, across a lifetime.
That is why they kept doing it.
It was a principle."
"Who was it," Iona said.
"Who was doing it.
Someone in the Balfour family for ninety years.
Was it always the same person, or was it many people." Rosa said, "That is what I am wondering too.
That is what I have been wondering for three years.
Now with these seven new books — maybe we can find out.
Mrs.
Balfour's daughter, the one who is clearing the farmhouse — I know her.
Her name is Ann.
She lives in Newton Stewart, twenty minutes away.
I could call her.
I could ask her."
"Please," said Iona.
"Please call her.
I want to know." Rosa smiled a small smile.
She said, "I will call her tomorrow.
Come back after school.
We will talk to her together.
If she is willing."
That evening Iona walked home.
She was quiet at supper.
Her parents noticed.
Her father asked what she was thinking about.
Iona said, "A book mystery.
A ninety-year-old book mystery." Her father laughed.
He said, "Well.
That is a good sort of mystery.
Better than most." And he did not press.
He knew about the bookshop.
He knew Iona would tell him when she was ready.
Iona lay in bed for a long time that night.
She thought about the seven books.
She thought about the person tearing endings out.
She thought about — the third possibility Rosa had mentioned.
That someone might have thought endings were private.
That a book's real ending was the one you made in your head, not the one the author had put on the page.
She was not sure she agreed.
But she was — for a strange reason she could not name — moved by the idea.
She thought about all the endings of all the books she had ever read.
Some she had loved.
Some she had hated.
She had never thought that any of them belonged to her.
